analysis.one_liner: Gives people with disabilities a federal right to receive long-term care at home instead of institutions.
analysis.headline: The Disability Integration Act, backed by 38 Senate cosponsors including two Republicans, sat in committee without a hearing or vote for two years and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal discrimination for state governments and long-term care insurers to force people with disabilities into nursing homes or institutions when they could live independently with home- and community-based services. It bans waiting lists, cost caps, and eligibility screens that block community care, requires that community care be offered before anyone is institutionalized, and lets individuals sue in federal court to enforce these rights. States that meet their transition plans would get a bigger federal Medicaid match for home-based care.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities who need long-term services and supports — whether currently in institutions or at risk of being placed in one — gain a federally enforceable right to live at home with services, maximum control over their own care, and access to affordable, accessible integrated housing. Their families and informal caregivers get support programs. Home care workers benefit from a requirement that states pay rates adequate to maintain a sufficient workforce.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with disabilities needing long-term care

how_it_helps.text: Bars government entities and long-term care insurers from denying or limiting community-based services to anyone eligible for institutional placement — including through waiting lists, service or cost caps, and restrictive eligibility criteria — and requires that community care be offered before institutionalization, with regular notice to people already institutionalized.

Requires states to ensure enough affordable, accessible, integrated housing that is not disability-specific and not tied to receiving services, including preferences and set-asides for people transitioning out of institutions and funding for home modifications.
Treats a failure to pay rates adequate to support a sufficient home care workforce as discrimination, which would raise pay and job security for home care workers.

Gives individuals standing to sue in federal court for injunctive relief and damages, allows courts to appoint attorneys and waive fees, and authorizes Justice Department enforcement with civil penalties of up to $100,000 for a first violation and $200,000 for repeat violations.
Rewards complying states with a 5-percentage-point increase in the federal Medicaid match (FMAP) for home and community-based services, for up to 10 years.

analysis.who_pays: State Medicaid programs bear the main cost of building enough home- and community-based capacity to serve everyone eligible, and the federal government picks up part of it through the higher FMAP. Institutional care providers — nursing homes and similar facilities — would lose residents and funding as people shift to community settings. Private long-term care insurers face new mandates to cover and provide community-based services, and public entities face litigation and penalty exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: State Medicaid programs and nursing homes

drawbacks.text: States would face large new costs to expand community-based services and affordable accessible housing; the FMAP bonus covers only home and community-based spending tied to the transition plan, not the full price of building capacity, and states must maintain prior spending levels to keep the bonus.

Public entities and insurers would be exposed to private lawsuits seeking actual and punitive damages, plus Justice Department civil penalties of up to $200,000, which states would argue constrains their budget flexibility over Medicaid long-term care.

The bill requires states to guarantee sufficient affordable, accessible, integrated housing — a problem state governments do not fully control given housing shortages — with full compliance due within 12 years of enactment.
Private long-term care insurers face new obligations to provide community-based services on the same non-discrimination terms as governments, which would raise their costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and civil-rights-based: thousands of people with disabilities who today cannot get the home services they need to avoid or leave institutions would gain an enforceable right to live in the community, with supports and housing attached. The costs are real and mostly fall on state Medicaid budgets, which would need significant new investment even with the enhanced federal match, and on institutional providers whose business model depends on the status quo. The bill's transition structure — self-evaluations, transition plans, a 12-year compliance runway, and an FMAP incentive — is a genuine attempt to phase the cost, but a state that cannot or will not pay would face court orders instead. On balance, a substantive rights expansion whose price tag is the reason it sat untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Chuck Schumer introduced the bill on January 15, 2019 with 23 original cosponsors, including Republican Senator Cory Gardner, framing it as completing the promise of the Americans with Disabilities Act's integration mandate.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day.
Support grew to 38 cosponsors — 35 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the committee took no further action of any kind for the rest of the two-year Congress.
The bill died on January 3, 2021 when the 116th Congress ended, never having received a hearing or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State Medicaid budgets and institutional care providers are better off because the bill died — they avoid the cost of shifting services out of nursing homes and the litigation exposure. People with disabilities who need long-term care, and the home care workforce, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and nursing homes avoided new obligations

for.name: Chuck Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 23 original cosponsors and recruited support that grew to 38 cosponsors.

for.name: 38 Senate cosponsors
for.role: Bipartisan group of senators (35 D, 2 R, 1 I)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it never reached a floor vote.

for.name: Cory Gardner
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

for.name: Disability rights organizations
for.role: National disability advocacy groups, including ADAPT
for.what_they_did: Championed the Disability Integration Act as the top legislative priority for community living rights and pressed for its passage.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, to which the bill was referred, held no hearing, took no markup, and never reported the bill during the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Controlled the Senate agenda in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or scheduled action on it at any point in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 35 of 38 cosponsors were Democrats, with 2 Republicans and 1 Independent — but no vote ever occurred, so the opposition never had to take a public position.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill shifts Medicaid long-term care dollars and residents away from institutional settings toward home and community-based services, threatening the revenue base of facilities that depend on institutional placement. Its interest in stopping the bill runs directly against the disabled people it serves.

industries.industry: Home care and community-based services providers and workers
industries.note: Community-based services would become a federally protected entitlement-like right, and states must pay rates adequate to sustain a sufficient workforce — expanding demand for, and raising pay in, home care. This is the industry the bill builds up.

The bill applies its non-discrimination and service mandates to any private entity that funds long-term services and supports, forcing insurers to cover and provide community-based care they could otherwise restrict or cap.

States take on major new service, housing, and planning obligations with a 12-year runway, but compliant states get a 5-point boost in the federal Medicaid match for home and community-based services. State budget officials were the most likely institutional constituency against the bill, though none is named in the record.
